title: A US penny cost 3.69 cents to make, so in 2025 the Mint stopped making them

cover.alt: A heap of copper-coloured US one-cent coins showing Lincoln's profile.

body: A one-cent coin has been worth less than the metal and labour that go into it for years. According to the US Mint, each penny cost **3.69 cents** to make in 2024, when it struck about 3.2 billion of them and lost $85.3 million doing so. Since 1982 the coin has been 97.5% zinc with a thin copper plating, replacing the mostly-copper cents of earlier decades. In February 2025 the president said he had ordered the Treasury to stop producing pennies; by May the Mint had stopped buying blanks, and the last penny for general circulation was struck in Philadelphia on 12 November 2025. The penny remains legal tender, with an estimated quarter of a trillion still in circulation, and the Mint still strikes some for collectors. The nickel loses money too, at 13.78 cents per 5-cent coin.

slides.question: In 2024, how many cents did it cost the Mint to make one penny?
slides.explanation: 3.69 cents, according to the Mint, on nearly 3.2 billion pennies: a loss of $85.3 million in a single year.

slides.question: What has a US penny mostly been made of since 1982?
